title: Hubble spies NGC 4394
caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 4394, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 4394 · constellation Coma Berenices · about 55 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Bright spiral arms, sprinkled with young blue stars, dark filaments of dust and fuzzy patches of star formation, spring from the ends of a bar that crosses the central bulge of NGC 4394. This barred spiral lies about 55 million light-years from Earth in Coma Berenices, Berenice's Hair, and is counted as part of the Virgo Cluster.

It is the textbook example of a barred spiral. At its centre sits a region of ionised gas called a LINER, whose spectrum shows a telltale set of emission lines, mostly from weakly ionised oxygen, nitrogen and sulphur.

LINERs are fairly common, but what powers them is still unclear. In most cases a central black hole is thought to be responsible, although lots of star formation could also do it. In NGC 4394, gravitational interaction with a neighbour has likely pushed gas into the centre, giving fresh fuel either to the black hole or to new stars.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.05 x 3.29 arcminutes) and distance (55 million light years), the frame spans roughly 49,000 × 53,000 light-years. Its light set out about 55 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's ACS and WFPC2 observed in blue and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures and near-infrared light reveal detail beyond the reach of the eye.

explore: The German–British astronomer William Herschel discovered NGC 4394 in 1784. The picture draws on data from more than one of Hubble's cameras, and the image credit acknowledges Judy Schmidt.
alt: A barred spiral galaxy whose bright arms, dotted with blue stars, dark dust and fuzzy star-forming patches, spring from the ends of a central bar.
